blocks.text: HarborWorks asks three questions about a topology: how many hops separate a source from each reachable vertex, how many disconnected groups exist in an undirected network, and whether a directed dependency cycle exists. All three involve traversal, but they do not share one interchangeable definition of visited state.

blocks.text: This chapter keeps those questions in separate functions. Breadth-first distances use discovery layers. Directed cycle detection distinguishes active recursion from completed work. Undirected components restart traversal from each unseen vertex under a symmetry precondition. The separation prevents a common error: taking a traversal that answers one question and assuming its boolean visited array answers every other graph question too.

Every vertex in layer d is removed before any vertex in layer d+1 that it discovers can get ahead of it. This is why a newly discovered neighbor receives the smallest possible hop count rather than merely the first arbitrary path length.

Use BFS for minimum hop count; use an algorithm with appropriate weight assumptions for minimum accumulated cost.

topics.title: 14.2 Performing Depth-First Search
topics.summary: Depth-first search follows one branch before returning to alternatives. Its state can be stored in language call frames or an explicit stack. A visited flag is enough for some reachability problems, but cycle detection in a directed graph needs to distinguish a current ancestor from a vertex whose exploration has finished.

topics.title: 14.2.1 Traversing Recursive Graph Structure
topics.summary: The directed traversal uses three colors: unseen, active, and finished. On entry it marks a vertex active. An edge to another active vertex closes a path back into the current recursion chain and therefore identifies a cycle. An edge to a finished vertex does not by itself prove a cycle; two branches may legitimately converge on completed work.

An explicit stack must retain both the current vertex and the next outgoing-edge position to reproduce active/finished transitions correctly; merely pushing all neighbors and marking them finished on push changes the meaning.

blocks.text: Depth-first search records a different kind of pending work. A recursive visit remains active until all of its outgoing neighbors have been considered. The active calls form a path through the exploration. This path is precisely the information needed to recognize a directed edge returning to an ancestor.

blocks.text: The color scheme uses unseen, active, and finished states. Unseen means no visit has started. Active means the vertex is on the current unfinished recursion path. Finished means all outgoing exploration for that call has completed. An edge to an active vertex creates a directed cycle; an edge to a finished vertex can simply be convergence on already explored work.

blocks.text: Consider a directed acyclic graph with edges zero-to-one, zero-to-two, and one-to-two. DFS can finish two while exploring one, then later encounter zero-to-two. A simple “already visited means cycle” rule would falsely reject this graph. The active/finished distinction preserves the difference between a back edge and harmless convergence.

reading.title: 14.2.1 Traversing Recursive Graph Structure
paragraphs: The directed traversal uses three colors: unseen, active, and finished. On entry it marks a vertex active. An edge to another active vertex closes a path back into the current recursion chain and therefore identifies a cycle. An edge to a finished vertex does not by itself prove a cycle; two branches may legitimately converge on completed work.

After every outgoing neighbor has been considered without finding a cycle, the vertex becomes finished. The outer loop starts a traversal at each still-unseen vertex so disconnected regions are not ignored. An empty graph has no directed cycle, while a self-loop reaches the current active vertex immediately.

Recursive depth can grow with the longest explored path. A large adversarial dependency chain may exhaust the native stack even though the algorithm is O(V+E). An explicit stack must retain both the current vertex and the next outgoing-edge position to reproduce active/finished transitions correctly; merely pushing all neighbors and marking them finished on push changes the meaning.

Depth-first search records a different kind of pending work. A recursive visit remains active until all of its outgoing neighbors have been considered. The active calls form a path through the exploration. This path is precisely the information needed to recognize a directed edge returning to an ancestor.

The color scheme uses unseen, active, and finished states. Unseen means no visit has started. Active means the vertex is on the current unfinished recursion path. Finished means all outgoing exploration for that call has completed. An edge to an active vertex creates a directed cycle; an edge to a finished vertex can simply be convergence on already explored work.

Consider a directed acyclic graph with edges zero-to-one, zero-to-two, and one-to-two. DFS can finish two while exploring one, then later encounter zero-to-two. A simple “already visited means cycle” rule would falsely reject this graph. The active/finished distinction preserves the difference between a back edge and harmless convergence.

Recursive depth can be linear in the number of vertices for a long chain. The original function is a compact teaching implementation, not a hardened importer for arbitrarily deep untrusted graphs. An explicit frame stack can preserve the same state machine without relying on one C++ call frame per vertex. The appendix’s traversal lab demonstrates that adaptation.

When translating to frames, remember which outgoing edge comes next. A stack of vertex identifiers alone can lose the distinction between entering a vertex and finishing it. Marking a vertex finished immediately after pushing its neighbors would destroy the active-path information that the cycle proof uses.

Cycle detection across the whole graph must start a new DFS from every unseen vertex. A cycle in a disconnected directed region should still be found. Restricting traversal to one source answers a narrower reachability-scoped question and must be named accordingly.

paragraphs: A shortest reconstructed path is 0→1→3 under the fixture’s neighbor order. Reconstruction must stop at the source and must not follow a predecessor for an unreachable vertex. A cycle outside the first traversal must still be detected. An iterative frame can contain a vertex and next-neighbor index; mark active on initial entry and finished only after that frame has exhausted its adjacency list.

Why distinguish active and finished in directed DFS? Only an active ancestor establishes the relevant back-edge cycle. Why can the undirected component routine reject no asymmetric input itself? Its current validator checks only indices; symmetry is a separate precondition. Why do iterative frames store a next-edge position? They must preserve unfinished recursive work and the correct finish event.
